A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SocialJax and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained content can be matched across the appendix renumbering and layout changes, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original training curves, simulation and training-speed measurements, cooperation metrics, SVO sweeps, and empirical Schelling diagrams.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated VDN and IPPO-RE baselines, reward-exchange sensitivity results, and 20-agent throughput measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 extends the implemented training options with VDN and IPPO-RE. IPPO-RE changes the training utility by combining an agent's reward with redistributed rewards from co-players. The environment dynamics and original IPPO, MAPPO, and SVO definitions are retained, making this a bounded extension of the suite.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine SocialJax games. The new taxonomy and difficulty tables classify existing environments; the 20-agent throughput tests vary scale within retained games rather than introducing another task or domain.

E2.justification: v3 adds VDN and IPPO-RE to the actual training-curve comparisons in Figure 2 and cooperation-metric comparisons in Table 3, substantially broadening the algorithm comparison. Table 3 also removes SVO-0°, although its return results remain in Table 2. The runtime comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments evaluate reward-exchange ratios of 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 alongside individual and common rewards, and select the smallest ratio reaching 95% of the best return. Appendix B.5 adds random-action throughput tests with 20 agents in seven environments. Existing hyperparameter tables, cooperation metrics, and the 30-episode Schelling evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 4 add a substantive sensitivity analysis asking how much reward exchange each environment needs and when partial sharing helps. Appendix B.5 and Table 7 additionally test throughput scalability with more agents. The earlier SVO sweeps, parameter-sharing comparisons, and Schelling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports means with standard deviations, and Section 4.3 explicitly mentions variation across seeds. v2 had shaded training curves without a corresponding uncertainty definition and example configurations specifying NUM_SEEDS=1. Those configurations remain unchanged; v3 does not specify the new study's run count or establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds VDN/IPPO-RE curves and metric entries, reward-ratio results, and 20-agent throughput results, while removing Table 3's SVO-0° entries. New Table 4 reports Clean Up returns of 1780 ± 340 at ratio 0.5 versus 970 ± 90 with common reward. Table 1 revises all four Clean Up JAX throughput values, including 2.1 million to 610,000 steps/second at 4096 environments, without explaining the revision. All 45 Table 2 returns are unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds the mathematical definition of reward-exchange utility and relates self-interest to individual/common-reward endpoints and intermediate ratios. The sequential-social-dilemma conditions, SVO equations, and appendix environment equations are retained. No theorem or proof is added; the new taxonomy is qualitative.

C1.justification: The introduction broadens the implementation contribution to explicitly include VDN and IPPO-RE. The central claims about an efficient JAX social-dilemma suite, at least 50-fold training acceleration, behavioral metrics, and Schelling validation remain unchanged in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantial interpretations involving credit assignment, free-riding, environment-specific reward-sharing requirements, and VDN's linear decomposition limitations. Appendices B.3–B.5 add qualitative dilemma and difficulty classifications and a parallelism-based scalability explanation. v2's proposed future taxonomy becomes a present classification, while formal self-interest estimation is newly deferred to future work.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds an explicit statement that datasets and model configurations are available in the existing repository; Appendix B.5 documents scalability and fixed-design exceptions. Existing API examples and IPPO/MAPPO/SVO hyperparameters are retained. The new Table 6 lists five Prisoner's Dilemma agents while the retained description specifies four, leaving that documentation inconsistent rather than establishing an actual setting change.

R1.justification: v3 adds Du et al.'s cooperation review, Zhang et al.'s mechanism-design work, Sunehag et al.'s VDN, and Willis et al.'s 2024 and 2025 reward-transfer/self-interest work. These provide limited additional positioning around the new algorithms and interpretations. The relationship to Melting Pot and JaxMARL remains substantially unchanged; numerous other reference edits update bibliographic metadata.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized wording corrections, updated author and affiliation information, new algorithm and analysis paragraphs, an ethics/reproducibility/LLM-use appendix, and additional appendix subsections. The scientific additions do not amount to extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The comparative displays expand substantially: Figure 1 labels and reorders retained screenshots, Figure 2 is redrawn with additional curves and legends, Table 3 changes comparator columns, and new Tables 4–7 display sensitivity, taxonomy, difficulty, and scalability information. Conference formatting also redistributes figures and tables; the old hyperparameter tables are retained as Tables 8–10.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the benchmark more useful through broader algorithm comparisons, reward-exchange sensitivity results with explicit variability, and agent-scaling evidence. These extend v2's already substantial validation. The benefit is limited by unspecified run counts, removal of the SVO-0° cooperation-metric column, and inconsistent scalability reporting: Clean Up is faster in the new 20-agent table than in the revised default-agent table despite the stated slowdown. Overall, the additions provide a limited net quality improvement.
